column1: What is intellectual property (IP)?
column2: IP covers non-physical creations that you cannot touch, such as ideas, brands, styles, and designs.

column1: What is the primary UK law that gives creators rights over their music, film, and graphics?
column2: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (1988).

column1: What is the primary UK law that protects trademarks such as logos and slogans?
column2: The Trade Marks Act (1994).

column1: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (1988) allow creators to do?
column2: It gives them the right to control the ways in which their material may be used and protects them from copying without permission.

column1: In the Vanilla Ice case study, which song's bass line was sampled without permission for 'Ice Ice Baby'?
column2: The song was 'Under Pressure' by David Bowie and Queen.

column1: What are the three steps required to legally use a copyrighted asset?
column2: Find the owner, contact them for permission, and potentially pay for a licence.

column1: For audio, music, and photos, how long does copyright typically last?
column2: It lasts for 70 years from when the work was first published.

column1: How long does copyright last for films?
column2: It lasts for 70 years after the death of the director, scriptwriter, and composer.

column1: For TV and radio broadcasts, what is the duration of copyright protection?
column2: Copyright lasts for 50 years from the date of the first broadcast.

column1: When is a creative work automatically copyrighted?
column2: A work is automatically copyrighted as soon as it is produced in a tangible form.

column1: What three pieces of information are helpful to include in a copyright statement?
column2: The copyright symbol (©), the year of publication, and the name of the author/creator.

column1: Does 'royalty free' mean an asset is free to use?
column2: No, it means a one-off licence fee is paid to use the asset, rather than paying a royalty for each use.

column1: What is a Creative Commons licence?
column2: It is a set of copyright licences that allow assets to be used for free, but only in certain specified ways.

column1: What is the one condition that all Creative Commons licences require?
column2: They always expect that you acknowledge who authored or created the asset.

column1: What does the Creative Commons 'Attribution' symbol (a person icon) mean?
column2: You must acknowledge who produced the asset.

column1: What does the Creative Commons 'Non-commercial' symbol (a crossed-out dollar or euro sign) prohibit?
column2: It prohibits the use of the asset for commercial purposes.

column1: The Creative Commons 'Share alike' symbol (a circular arrow) means that others can create _____ of this asset.
column2: derivatives (alterations)

column1: What does the Creative Commons 'No derivates' symbol (an equals sign in a circle) mean?
column2: No derivatives or alterations of the original asset are allowed.

column1: What type of intellectual property do patents protect?
column2: Patents are used to protect inventions.

column1: What are the three criteria an invention must meet to be granted a patent?
column2: It must be new, be inventive (not an obvious change), and be for something that is made or used.

column1: What is the maximum duration for which a patent can last?
column2: A patent can last for up to 20 years.

column1: Name two types of creations that cannot be patented.
column2: Any two from: books/plays/music/artwork, medical treatments, scientific theories, or the presentation of information.

column1: Can the 'idea' for a television quiz show be protected by copyright law?
column2: No, you cannot protect ideas using copyright law.

column1: While an idea for a quiz show cannot be copyrighted, what specific components of the show can be?
column2: The music, styling of the set, graphics, and voiceover scripts can all be individually copyrighted.

column1: What is the term for the exceptions to copyright law that allow limited use of works without permission?
column2: Fair dealing.

column1: Under 'fair dealing', what is a common reason for which you can copy parts of a work?
column2: For non-commercial research or private study.

column1: What is the main limitation of 'fair dealing' when copying a work for private study?
column2: You cannot copy the whole work, as this would not be considered fair.

column1: What is the purpose of using a watermark on images and videos?
column2: Watermarks show that a licence has not yet been paid for and deter illegal copying.

column1: What type of intellectual property protects logos, symbols, or slogans that identify a product or service?
column2: Trademarks.

column1: What does the 'TM' symbol (™) indicate?
column2: It indicates that the owner is claiming a word, logo, or slogan as a trademark.

column1: What does the '®' symbol indicate?
column2: It indicates that a trademark has been officially registered at the UK Intellectual Property Office (UKIPO).

column1: Why couldn't Asda® register the phrase 'SPEC SAVINGS AT ASDA' as a trademark?
column2: It was considered too similar to the existing Specsavers® registered trademark.

column1: When producing a compilation album of famous songs, what must the producer do regarding copyright for each song?
column2: They must contact each copyright owner, get permission, and pay a royalty or fee for each song.

column1: Intellectual property covers items that aren't physical, such as graphics, video, music, and _____.
column2: ideas, brands, styles and designs

column1: What must a user keep a record of after getting permission to use a copyrighted asset?
column2: A record of permissions granted.

column1: What is a potential reason a copyright owner might refuse permission to use their work?
column2: If the proposed use is controversial or may damage their own brand or reputation.

column1: What is a payment made to an author or creator for each copy of their work sold, such as on a DVD?
column2: A royalty.

column1: For a patent to be granted, the invention must be new, meaning it has never been described _____ anywhere in the world.
column2: publicly

column1: Software for a self-driving car could be patented, but what kind of software is generally not patentable?
column2: Non-technical software, for example, a car game.
